warmup.q: A hot loop calls rule.fee(amount). For weeks only CardFee and SepaFee reach that call. Then a WalletFee starts taking a third of the traffic. What does C2 most likely do with that call site?
options: Nothing changes: the compiled code already handles any FeeRule
It throws the compiled code away and recompiles the call as a plain virtual call, with nothing inlined
It inlines all three implementations, because they are small
It stops compiling the method and leaves it in the interpreter for good
warmup.why: C2 inlined the two types it had seen behind type checks, and compiled "any other type" as an uncommon trap. The first wallet trips the trap, the code is made not entrant, and the recompile sees three types with no 90% winner. That is a megamorphic site: a virtual call each time. It still works, just without inlining.

sections.h: Inlining copies the callee into the caller, inside a bytecode budget
sections.html:
Inlining means C2 pastes the body of a called method into the caller and compiles them as one piece. Saving the call is the small win. The big win is that C2's other optimizations work inside one compiled unit, and now they can see both sides of the call: escape analysis (proving an object never leaves the method, so it needn't be allocated on the heap), constant folding (computing results from known values at compile time) and loop optimizations such as unrolling. A method that isn't inlined is a wall C2 can't see through.

C2 decides per call site (one call instruction in the bytecode), using the callee's bytecode size (the (N bytes) from lesson 1). The rule in HotSpot's bytecodeInfo.cpp is short. C2 divides how often the call site ran by how often the caller was invoked. If the call runs on at least 25% of the caller's invocations (InlineFrequencyRatio), the site counts as hot and the limit is 325 bytes (FreqInlineSize). Otherwise the limit is 35 bytes (MaxInlineSize). There is also a depth limit of 15 levels, and a callee that is already compiled into more than 2,500 bytes of machine code (InlineSmallCode) is refused. These values are the same from JDK 21 to JDK 27.

The budget counts every byte, including code that almost never runs. Here is a guard that checks an amount on every refund. It builds its error message inline:

Java
static long requireAmountInline(long cents) {
    if (cents <= 0 || cents > MAX_CENTS) {
        throw new IllegalArgumentException(
                String.format("amount must be between 1 and %d cents, got %d", MAX_CENTS, cents));
    }
    return cents;
}
Kotlin
fun requireAmountInline(cents: Long): Long {
    if (cents <= 0 || cents > MAX_CENTS) {
        throw IllegalArgumentException("amount must be between 1 and %d cents, got %d".format(MAX_CENTS, cents))
    }
    return cents
}

The Java version is 49 bytes. Move the message into its own method and the hot method shrinks to 21:

Java
static long requireAmount(long cents) {
    if (cents <= 0 || cents > MAX_CENTS) throw badAmount(cents);   // hot path: 21 bytes
    return cents;
}

static IllegalArgumentException badAmount(long cents) {            // cold path, its own method
    return new IllegalArgumentException(
            String.format("amount must be between 1 and %d cents, got %d", MAX_CENTS, cents));
}
Kotlin
fun requireAmount(cents: Long): Long {
    if (cents <= 0 || cents > MAX_CENTS) throw badAmount(cents)    // hot path: 21 bytes
    return cents
}

fun badAmount(cents: Long) =                                        // cold path, its own function
    IllegalArgumentException("amount must be between 1 and %d cents, got %d".format(MAX_CENTS, cents))

In the demo below, each guard runs on 1 call in 8, so neither site is hot. This is the real C2 output:

@ 15   ...InliningDemo::requireAmountInline (49 bytes)   too big
@ 30   ...InliningDemo::requireAmountSplit (21 bytes)   inline (hot)

Don't read too much into inline (hot). It's simply the message C2 prints when it inlines and has nothing more specific to say. The JDK's own code uses this split all the time: a small check, and a separate method that builds the exception.

try.title: See C2 refuse the big guard
steps: Run InliningDemo. It starts a second JVM with -XX:+UnlockDiagnosticVMOptions -XX:+PrintInlining and keeps the lines about refund.
Find the decisions under the tier 3 compile (C1 says callee is too large) and under the tier 4 compile (C2 says too big).
Run the Kotlin twin. Compare the size of requireAmountInline in both languages.

code.title: InliningDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.performance.l02; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; /** * Two versions of the same amount check. One builds its error message inline, the other moves * the cold path into a helper. Run it: a second JVM starts with -XX:+PrintInlining and the demo * prints what C1 and C2 decided at the two call sites in refund(). */ public class InliningDemo { static final long MAX_CENTS = 100_000_000L; // the error message is built right here, so its bytecode counts against the inlining budget static long requireAmountInline(long cents) { if (cents <= 0 || cents > MAX_CENTS) { throw new IllegalArgumentException( String.format("amount must be between 1 and %d cents, got %d", MAX_CENTS, cents)); } return cents; } // same check, but the cold path lives in its own method static long requireAmountSplit(long cents) { if (cents <= 0 || cents > MAX_CENTS) throw badAmount(cents); return cents; } static IllegalArgumentException badAmount(long cents) { return new IllegalArgumentException( String.format("amount must be between 1 and %d cents, got %d", MAX_CENTS, cents)); } // each check runs on 1 call in 8, so neither call site counts as hot for C2 static long refund(long cents, int i) { long r = cents / 2; if ((i & 7) == 0) r += requireAmountInline(cents); if ((i & 7) == 1) r += requireAmountSplit(cents); return r; } static void work() { long s = 0; for (int i = 0; i < 2_000_000; i++) s += refund(1_000 + (i & 1023), i); System.out.println("checksum " + s); } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { if (args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("child")) { work(); return; } String java = ProcessHandle.current().info().command().orElse("java"); List<String> cmd = new ArrayList<>(List.of(java, "-XX:+UnlockDiagnosticVMOptions", "-XX:+PrintInlining", "-XX:+PrintCompilation", "-cp", System.getProperty("java.class.path"), InliningDemo.class.getName(), "child")); Process p = new ProcessBuilder(cmd).redirectErrorStream(true).start(); try (var out = p.inputReader()) { // keep the compile lines for refund() and the decisions about the two checks out.lines() .filter(l -> l.contains("InliningDemo::refund (") || l.contains("requireAmount") || l.startsWith("checksum")) .forEach(System.out::println); } p.waitFor(); } }

alt.title: InliningDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.performance.l02 // Kotlin twin of InliningDemo.java: the same two checks, compiled by kotlinc. // Run it: a second JVM starts with -XX:+PrintInlining and the demo prints the decisions in refund(). const val MAX_CENTS = 100_000_000L // the error message is built right here, so its bytecode counts against the inlining budget fun requireAmountInline(cents: Long): Long { if (cents <= 0 || cents > MAX_CENTS) { throw IllegalArgumentException("amount must be between 1 and %d cents, got %d".format(MAX_CENTS, cents)) } return cents } // same check, but the cold path lives in its own function fun requireAmountSplit(cents: Long): Long { if (cents <= 0 || cents > MAX_CENTS) throw badAmount(cents) return cents } fun badAmount(cents: Long) = IllegalArgumentException("amount must be between 1 and %d cents, got %d".format(MAX_CENTS, cents)) // each check runs on 1 call in 8, so neither call site counts as hot for C2 fun refund(cents: Long, i: Int): Long { var r = cents / 2 if ((i and 7) == 0) r += requireAmountInline(cents) if ((i and 7) == 1) r += requireAmountSplit(cents) return r } fun main(args: Array<String>) { if (args.firstOrNull() == "child") { var s = 0L for (i in 0 until 2_000_000) s += refund(1_000L + (i and 1023), i) println("checksum $s") return } val java = ProcessHandle.current().info().command().orElse("java") val p = ProcessBuilder(java, "-XX:+UnlockDiagnosticVMOptions", "-XX:+PrintInlining", "-XX:+PrintCompilation", "-cp", System.getProperty("java.class.path"), "workbench.performance.l02.InliningDemoKt", "child") .redirectErrorStream(true).start() p.inputReader().useLines { lines -> lines.filter { "InliningDemoKt::refund (" in it || "requireAmount" in it || it.startsWith("checksum") } .forEach(::println) } p.waitFor() }

try.expect: Both compilers refuse requireAmountInline and inline requireAmountSplit. In Java the sizes are 49 and 21 bytes. In Kotlin the inline-message version is 66 bytes: Kotlin's "...".format(...) is an inline function, so kotlinc pastes its body (an array copy and a null check) into the caller. The split version is 21 bytes in both.

sections.h: C2 bets on the receiver types it has seen
sections.html:
A call through an interface, like rule.fee(amount), could go to any implementation. C2 can only inline it if it knows which one. The object a method is called on is the receiver, so at tier 3 C1 records the receiver types it sees at every call site, and C2 reads that profile.

One type seen: C2 inlines that type's method behind a cheap class check. This is a monomorphic call site. Two types: it inlines both behind two checks (bimorphic). The profile keeps two types per site (TypeProfileWidth = 2). With three or more, C2 inlines only a type that has at least 90% of the calls (TypeProfileMajorReceiverPercent). Otherwise the site is megamorphic: C2 emits a plain virtual call (look up the method in the receiver's class at run time, then jump to it) and inlines nothing.

-XX:+PrintInlining shows the switch. These are real lines for the area() call in lesson 1's Hot program, before and after the new shapes arrived:

@ 27   Hot$Square::area (10 bytes)   inline (hot)
 \-> TypeProfile (977323/977323 counts) = Hot$Square

@ 27   Hot$Shape::area (0 bytes)   virtual call

The cost is more than the call. MegamorphicBench feeds one call site with 1, 2 or 3 fee-rule types, in batches of 1,024. In several runs on the shared 4-vCPU VM used for this course, one type took 0.2 to 0.4 µs per batch, two types 0.4 to 0.7 µs, and three types 3 to 4 µs. The error bars were wide on that noisy machine, but the jump at three types showed up in every run. With the calls inlined, C2 can optimize the whole loop. With a virtual call per element, it can't.

Notice what didn't matter. The fee-rule classes in the benchmark are final, and so are the records in Hot. C2 inlined Square::area because the profile said every receiver was a Square, not because of a modifier. Kotlin classes are final by default, and that doesn't change anything here either. What changes speed is how many types reach one call site.

try.title: Count the types at a call site
steps: Predict the three numbers before you run: ns per batch with 1, 2 and 3 types.
Run MegamorphicBench. It's a JMH benchmark (lesson 3 explains JMH). Each case runs in a fresh JVM, so each starts with a clean profile. It takes about 10 seconds.
Run it with -Pargs='1 4'. Does a fourth type cost more than the third? The Kotlin twin runs 1, 3 and 4 types.

code.title: MegamorphicBench.java
code.html: package workbench.performance.l02; import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.Benchmark; import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.BenchmarkMode; import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.Fork; import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.Measurement; import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.Mode; import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.OutputTimeUnit; import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.Param; import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.Scope; import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.Setup; import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.State; import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.Warmup; import org.openjdk.jmh.results.RunResult; import org.openjdk.jmh.runner.Runner; import org.openjdk.jmh.runner.options.OptionsBuilder; import org.openjdk.jmh.runner.options.VerboseMode; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; /** * One call site, fed 1, 2 or 3 receiver types (choose others with -Pargs='1 4'). JMH runs each case in a fresh JVM, * so every case starts with a clean type profile. Lesson 3 explains the annotations. */ @State(Scope.Thread) @BenchmarkMode(Mode.AverageTime) @OutputTimeUnit(TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS) @Warmup(iterations = 2, time = 200, timeUnit = TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS) @Measurement(iterations = 3, time = 200, timeUnit = TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS) @Fork(1) public class MegamorphicBench { interface FeeRule { long fee(long cents); } static final class Card implements FeeRule { public long fee(long c) { return c * 29 / 1000 + 30; } } static final class Sepa implements FeeRule { public long fee(long c) { return 35; } } static final class Wallet implements FeeRule { public long fee(long c) { return c * 15 / 1000 + 10; } } static final class Bnpl implements FeeRule { public long fee(long c) { return c * 45 / 1000; } } @Param({"1", "2", "3"}) int types; FeeRule[] rules; long amountCents = 12_345; // not final: lesson 3 explains why @Setup public void setup() { FeeRule[] kinds = {new Card(), new Sepa(), new Wallet(), new Bnpl()}; rules = new FeeRule[1024]; for (int i = 0; i < rules.length; i++) rules[i] = kinds[i % types]; } @Benchmark public long feesForBatch() { long sum = 0; for (FeeRule r : rules) sum += r.fee(amountCents); // the call site under test return sum; // returned, so JMH consumes it } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { var builder = new OptionsBuilder() .include(MegamorphicBench.class.getName()) .verbosity(VerboseMode.SILENT); if (args.length > 0) builder.param("types", args); // for example -Pargs='1 3 4' var options = builder.build(); System.out.println("types at the call site -> ns per batch of 1,024 fees"); for (RunResult r : new Runner(options).run()) { var s = r.getPrimaryResult(); System.out.printf(" %s type(s): %8.1f ns (+/- %.1f)%n", r.getParams().getParam("types"), s.getScore(), s.getScoreError()); } } }

alt.title: MegamorphicBench.kt
alt.html: package workbench.performance.l02 // JMH benchmarks must be Java classes in this lab (the annotation processor runs on Java only). // This Kotlin twin runs the same Java benchmark through JMH's Runner API. import org.openjdk.jmh.runner.Runner import org.openjdk.jmh.runner.options.OptionsBuilder import org.openjdk.jmh.runner.options.VerboseMode fun main() { val options = OptionsBuilder() .include(MegamorphicBench::class.java.name) .param("types", "1", "3", "4") // one type, three types, four types .verbosity(VerboseMode.SILENT) .build() println("types at the call site -> ns per batch of 1,024 fees") for (r in Runner(options).run()) { val s = r.primaryResult println(" %s type(s): %8.1f ns (+/- %.1f)".format(r.params.getParam("types"), s.score, s.scoreError)) } }

try.expect: One and two types are close, both a few hundred nanoseconds per batch. Three types cost several times more, around ten times on the course VM. Four types cost about the same as three: once the site is megamorphic, it's a virtual call either way. Expect wide error bars on a laptop with other work running.

sections.h: When a bet loses: uncommon traps and deoptimization
sections.html:
C2 compiles what the profile showed and nothing else. A branch that was never taken and a receiver type that never appeared don't get compiled code. In their place C2 puts an uncommon trap: a stub that hands the running frame back to the interpreter if that "impossible" case ever happens.

When a trap fires, the JVM deoptimizes: it rebuilds an interpreter frame from the compiled frame and carries on there. The compiled code is made not entrant. The method goes back to profiling, now with the new case in its profile, and gets compiled again. The figure shows the cycle.

DeoptDemo triggers both common kinds. It settles batches of card charges, then one refund appears, then SEPA and wallet payments arrive:

Java
long fee = methods[i].feeCents(amounts[i]);   // bytecode 20: which types has it seen?
if (refund[i]) net -= amounts[i];             // bytecode 31: has this branch ever been taken?
else net += amounts[i] - fee;
Kotlin
val fee = methods[i].feeCents(amounts[i])     // which types has it seen?
if (refund[i]) net -= amounts[i]              // has this branch ever been taken?
else net += amounts[i] - fee

The real log on JDK 25, trimmed to the important parts:

phase 2: one refund per batch
... DeoptDemo.settle(...) trap_bci=31 unstable_if reinterpret
81   23       4       ...DeoptDemo::settle (62 bytes)   made not entrant: uncommon trap
phase 3: SEPA and wallet payments arrive
... DeoptDemo.settle(...) trap_bci=20 class_check maybe_recompile
93   25       4       ...DeoptDemo::settle (62 bytes)   made not entrant: uncommon trap

unstable_if means a branch C2 had compiled as never taken: the refund. class_check means a type check failed at a call it had inlined for cards only. Each time, a new tier 4 compile follows within a few milliseconds.

This is normal, and cheap when it happens a few times. HotSpot also limits how often one method can go around the cycle (PerMethodRecompilationCutoff is 400 recompiles). Expect a burst of deoptimizations after a deploy, or when a new payment method gets its first traffic. A steady stream of them in a service that has been up for hours is worth a look. JFR has a ready-made view for it, deoptimizations-by-reason, which lesson 5 uses.

try.title: Trip a branch trap and a type trap
steps: Predict: in which phase will the first made not entrant for tier 4 code appear, and with which reason in the deoptimization log?
Run DeoptDemo. It starts a second JVM with -XX:+PrintCompilation -Xlog:deoptimization=debug.
Match each trap_bci to a line of settle (bytecode 20 is the feeCents call, 31 is the if (refund[i]) test). Then run the Kotlin twin: its bytecode indexes differ, the story doesn't.

code.title: DeoptDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.performance.l02; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; /** * Settles batches of payments in three phases: card charges only, then a refund appears, * then SEPA and wallet payments appear. Run it: a second JVM starts with -XX:+PrintCompilation * and -Xlog:deoptimization=debug, and the demo prints what happened to settle(). */ public class DeoptDemo { interface PaymentMethod { long feeCents(long amountCents); } record Card(long bps) implements PaymentMethod { public long feeCents(long a) { return a * bps / 10_000; } } record Sepa(long flat) implements PaymentMethod { public long feeCents(long a) { return flat; } } record Wallet(long bps, long flat) implements PaymentMethod { public long feeCents(long a) { return a * bps / 10_000 + flat; } } static long settle(PaymentMethod[] methods, long[] amounts, boolean[] refund) { long net = 0; for (int i = 0; i < amounts.length; i++) { long fee = methods[i].feeCents(amounts[i]); // call site: which types has it seen? if (refund[i]) net -= amounts[i]; // branch: has it ever been taken? else net += amounts[i] - fee; } return net; } static void work() { int n = 1_000; PaymentMethod[] methods = new PaymentMethod[n]; long[] amounts = new long[n]; boolean[] refund = new boolean[n]; for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) { methods[i] = new Card(290); amounts[i] = 1_000 + i; } long total = 0; System.out.println("phase 1: card charges only"); for (int r = 0; r < 3_000; r++) total += settle(methods, amounts, refund); System.out.println("phase 2: one refund per batch"); refund[500] = true; for (int r = 0; r < 3_000; r++) total += settle(methods, amounts, refund); System.out.println("phase 3: SEPA and wallet payments arrive"); for (int i = 0; i < n; i += 3) methods[i] = new Sepa(35); for (int i = 1; i < n; i += 3) methods[i] = new Wallet(150, 10); for (int r = 0; r < 3_000; r++) total += settle(methods, amounts, refund); System.out.println("done, checksum " + total); } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { if (args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("child")) { work(); return; } String java = ProcessHandle.current().info().command().orElse("java"); List<String> cmd = new ArrayList<>(List.of(java, "-XX:+PrintCompilation", "-Xlog:deoptimization=debug", "-cp", System.getProperty("java.class.path"), DeoptDemo.class.getName(), "child")); Process p = new ProcessBuilder(cmd).redirectErrorStream(true).start(); try (var out = p.inputReader()) { out.lines() .filter(l -> l.contains("DeoptDemo::settle") || l.contains("DeoptDemo.settle") || l.startsWith("phase") || l.startsWith("done")) .map(l -> l.replaceAll(" pc=.*", "")) // drop machine addresses .forEach(System.out::println); } p.waitFor(); } }

alt.html: package workbench.performance.l02 // Kotlin twin of DeoptDemo.java: card charges only, then a refund appears, then SEPA and wallet payments. // Run it: a second JVM starts with -XX:+PrintCompilation and -Xlog:deoptimization=debug. interface PaymentMethod { fun feeCents(amountCents: Long): Long } class CardFee(private val bps: Long) : PaymentMethod { override fun feeCents(amountCents: Long) = amountCents * bps / 10_000 } class SepaFee(private val flat: Long) : PaymentMethod { override fun feeCents(amountCents: Long) = flat } class WalletFee(private val bps: Long, private val flat: Long) : PaymentMethod { override fun feeCents(amountCents: Long) = amountCents * bps / 10_000 + flat } fun settle(methods: Array<PaymentMethod>, amounts: LongArray, refund: BooleanArray): Long { var net = 0L for (i in amounts.indices) { val fee = methods[i].feeCents(amounts[i]) // call site: which types has it seen? if (refund[i]) net -= amounts[i] // branch: has it ever been taken? else net += amounts[i] - fee } return net } private fun work() { val n = 1_000 val methods = Array<PaymentMethod>(n) { CardFee(290) } val amounts = LongArray(n) { 1_000L + it } val refund = BooleanArray(n) var total = 0L println("phase 1: card charges only") repeat(3_000) { total += settle(methods, amounts, refund) } println("phase 2: one refund per batch") refund[500] = true repeat(3_000) { total += settle(methods, amounts, refund) } println("phase 3: SEPA and wallet payments arrive") for (i in 0 until n step 3) methods[i] = SepaFee(35) for (i in 1 until n step 3) methods[i] = WalletFee(150, 10) repeat(3_000) { total += settle(methods, amounts, refund) } println("done, checksum $total") } fun main(args: Array<String>) { if (args.firstOrNull() == "child") return work() val java = ProcessHandle.current().info().command().orElse("java") val p = ProcessBuilder(java, "-XX:+PrintCompilation", "-Xlog:deoptimization=debug", "-cp", System.getProperty("java.class.path"), "workbench.performance.l02.DeoptDemoKt", "child") .redirectErrorStream(true).start() p.inputReader().useLines { lines -> lines.filter { "DeoptDemoKt::settle" in it || "DeoptDemoKt.settle" in it || it.startsWith("phase") || it.startsWith("done") } .map { it.replace(Regex(" pc=.*"), "") } // drop machine addresses .forEach(::println) } p.waitFor() }

try.expect: Phase 1 compiles settle up to tier 4, including an OSR version. Phase 2 prints unstable_if at trap_bci=31 and retires the tier 4 code, then recompiles. Phase 3 prints class_check at trap_bci=20, retires it again and recompiles. On JDK 25 the PrintCompilation lines end in made not entrant: uncommon trap; on JDK 21 they just say made not entrant.

sections.h: Intrinsics: JDK methods the JIT swaps for hand-written code
sections.html:
Some JDK methods never run as their Java code once they're hot. HotSpot has hand-written machine code, or hand-written compiler IR (the compiler's internal form of a program), for them. These are intrinsics. In the JDK source they carry @IntrinsicCandidate, whose Javadoc says the method "may be (but is not guaranteed to be) intrinsified". PrintInlining marks them:

java.lang.Long::bitCount (61 bytes)   (intrinsic)
java.lang.Math::addExact (32 bytes)   (intrinsic)
java.util.Arrays::equals (43 bytes)   (intrinsic)

Those are real lines from IntrinsicsDemo. Long.bitCount is 61 bytes of shifts and masks in Java, and on x86 C2 replaces it with one POPCNT instruction. Arrays.equals on byte arrays ends up in ArraysSupport.vectorizedMismatch, which reads 8 bytes at a time even in its Java version, and is an intrinsic as well. The bytecode size doesn't matter for an intrinsic, because that Java code isn't what runs.

The practical rule: in hot code, call the JDK method instead of writing the loop yourself. For money in cents, Math.addExact and Math.multiplyExact give you overflow checks that throw ArithmeticException, and both are intrinsics. A hand-written loop that compares two idempotency keys byte by byte gives up the 8-bytes-at-a-time path that Arrays.equals gets for free, and it's more code to get wrong.

Kotlin gets the same intrinsics, because its standard library calls these JDK methods. ByteArray.contentEquals calls java.util.Arrays.equals, and Long.countOneBits() calls java.lang.Long.bitCount:

Java
long total = Math.addExact(a, b);                 // ArithmeticException on overflow
boolean same = Arrays.equals(keyA, keyB);
int flags = Long.bitCount(riskMask);
Kotlin
val total = Math.addExact(a, b)                   // ArithmeticException on overflow
val same = keyA.contentEquals(keyB)               // calls java.util.Arrays.equals

try.title: List the intrinsics in a hot loop
steps: Run IntrinsicsDemo. It prints the PrintInlining lines for the three JDK methods it calls.
Run the Kotlin twin, which uses contentEquals and countOneBits instead of calling Arrays and Long directly.
Optional: run the Java demo's child JVM yourself with -XX:+PrintInlining and grep for intrinsic to see how many others the JDK uses on its own.

code.title: IntrinsicsDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.performance.l02; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.Arrays; import java.util.List; import java.util.TreeSet; /** * Calls three JDK methods that HotSpot replaces with hand-written machine code. Run it: a second * JVM starts with -XX:+PrintInlining and the demo lists the intrinsic decisions for them. */ public class IntrinsicsDemo { static long totalCents(long[] cents) { long sum = 0; for (long c : cents) sum = Math.addExact(sum, c); // throws on overflow instead of wrapping return sum; } static boolean sameKey(byte[] a, byte[] b) { return Arrays.equals(a, b); // compares many bytes per step } static int riskFlags(long mask) { return Long.bitCount(mask); // one POPCNT instruction on x86 } static void work() { long[] cents = new long[1_000]; Arrays.fill(cents, 1_999); byte[] k1 = new byte[64], k2 = new byte[64]; long s = 0; for (int i = 0; i < 200_000; i++) { s += totalCents(cents); if (sameKey(k1, k2)) s++; s += riskFlags(i); } System.out.println("checksum " + s); } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { if (args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("child")) { work(); return; } String java = ProcessHandle.current().info().command().orElse("java"); List<String> cmd = new ArrayList<>(List.of(java, "-XX:+UnlockDiagnosticVMOptions", "-XX:+PrintInlining", "-cp", System.getProperty("java.class.path"), IntrinsicsDemo.class.getName(), "child")); Process p = new ProcessBuilder(cmd).redirectErrorStream(true).start(); TreeSet<String> seen = new TreeSet<>(); try (var out = p.inputReader()) { out.lines() .filter(l -> l.contains("intrinsic")) .filter(l -> l.contains("Math::addExact") || l.contains("Arrays::equals") || l.contains("Long::bitCount")) .map(l -> l.replaceFirst("^\\s*@ \\d+\\s+", "")) // drop the indent and the call-site index .forEach(seen::add); } p.waitFor(); seen.forEach(System.out::println); } }

alt.title: IntrinsicsDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.performance.l02 // Kotlin twin of IntrinsicsDemo.java. The Kotlin standard library calls the same JDK methods, // so the same intrinsics apply: contentEquals calls Arrays.equals, countOneBits calls Long.bitCount. fun totalCentsKt(cents: LongArray): Long { var sum = 0L for (c in cents) sum = Math.addExact(sum, c) // throws on overflow instead of wrapping return sum } fun sameKeyKt(a: ByteArray, b: ByteArray) = a.contentEquals(b) fun riskFlagsKt(mask: Long) = mask.countOneBits() fun main(args: Array<String>) { if (args.firstOrNull() == "child") { val cents = LongArray(1_000) { 1_999 } val k1 = ByteArray(64) val k2 = ByteArray(64) var s = 0L for (i in 0 until 200_000) { s += totalCentsKt(cents) if (sameKeyKt(k1, k2)) s++ s += riskFlagsKt(i.toLong()) } println("checksum $s") return } val java = ProcessHandle.current().info().command().orElse("java") val p = ProcessBuilder(java, "-XX:+UnlockDiagnosticVMOptions", "-XX:+PrintInlining", "-cp", System.getProperty("java.class.path"), "workbench.performance.l02.IntrinsicsDemoKt", "child") .redirectErrorStream(true).start() val seen = sortedSetOf<String>() p.inputReader().useLines { lines -> lines.filter { "intrinsic" in it } .filter { "Math::addExact" in it || "Arrays::equals" in it || "Long::bitCount" in it } .mapTo(seen) { it.replaceFirst(Regex("""^\s*@ \d+\s+"""), "") } // drop the indent and call-site index } p.waitFor() seen.forEach(::println) }

try.expect: Both programs print the same three lines, each ending in (intrinsic): Long::bitCount, Math::addExact and Arrays::equals. Kotlin's standard library functions disappear entirely: they are inline, so the call in the bytecode is already the JDK method.

analogy: Think of a routing switch at a payment processor. If almost every transaction it has seen is Visa, it keeps a fast lane wired straight to the Visa network and sends anything else to a slow manual desk. Two networks still fit: two fast lanes. When it has seen five networks with no clear winner, it stops keeping fast lanes and looks up each transaction's route in a table. That's a megamorphic call site. When the first Amex arrives at a switch wired only for Visa, it goes to the manual desk, and the switch gets rewired with Amex in mind (an uncommon trap, then a recompile). The analogy breaks on cost: a real switch pays for each manual review, while the JVM pays once per trap and then rebuilds the fast path.
world: Payment code is full of interfaces with a handful of implementations: PaymentMethod, FeeRule, RiskCheck, Kafka Deserializers. When a hot loop in your settlement job calls through one of them and three or more implementations reach the same call site, that call becomes a virtual call and the loop around it loses its optimizations. You won't see that in a code review. You'll see it in a profile (lessons 5 and 6) or in a JMH run. Also expect a short burst of deoptimizations when a new payment method goes live, since the first wallet payment trips traps compiled for cards only. That burst is fine. A steady stream hours later is a signal to check jfr view deoptimizations-by-reason.
mistake: The common mistake is adding final to classes and methods to make calls faster. Part of the confusion is that final does matter for fields, as lesson 3 shows. For calls, C2 decides from the type profile. It inlined Square::area because every receiver it saw was a Square, and the third record type still turned the call into a virtual call, final or not. Kotlin's final-by-default classes behave the same way. If a profile shows a hot megamorphic call, measure it with JMH first. Then reduce the number of types that reach that one call site, or keep the hot callee small so it inlines wherever the type is known.

compare.title: The same guard, before and after the split

java.title: InliningDemo.java
java.html: // before: 49 bytes, "too big" at a site that isn't hot static long requireAmountInline(long cents) { if (cents <= 0 || cents > MAX_CENTS) { throw new IllegalArgumentException( String.format("amount must be between 1 and %d cents, got %d", MAX_CENTS, cents)); } return cents; } // after: 21 bytes, inlined static long requireAmount(long cents) { if (cents <= 0 || cents > MAX_CENTS) throw badAmount(cents); // hot path: 21 bytes return cents; } static IllegalArgumentException badAmount(long cents) { // cold path, its own method return new IllegalArgumentException( String.format("amount must be between 1 and %d cents, got %d", MAX_CENTS, cents)); }

kotlin.title: InliningDemo.kt
kotlin.html: // before: 66 bytes, "too big" at a site that isn't hot fun requireAmountInline(cents: Long): Long { if (cents <= 0 || cents > MAX_CENTS) { throw IllegalArgumentException("amount must be between 1 and %d cents, got %d".format(MAX_CENTS, cents)) } return cents } // after: 21 bytes, inlined fun requireAmount(cents: Long): Long { if (cents <= 0 || cents > MAX_CENTS) throw badAmount(cents) // hot path: 21 bytes return cents } fun badAmount(cents: Long) = // cold path, its own function IllegalArgumentException("amount must be between 1 and %d cents, got %d".format(MAX_CENTS, cents))

compare.note: After the split, both languages compile requireAmount to the same 21 bytes, and C2 treats them the same. Before the split, the Kotlin version is 66 bytes against Java's 49. Kotlin's String.format extension is an inline function, so kotlinc copies its body into the caller: an Arrays.copyOf of the arguments and a null check. Kotlin inline removes a call at compile time, but the pasted bytecode counts against the JIT's budget for the method that received it. Use inline for small higher-order functions, and keep big bodies out of hot methods in either language.

worked.title: Find out why a hot method isn't inlined, and fix it

steps.say: A refund handler is slower than expected in a profile. Start the service with the diagnostic flags and look for your method in the inlining log.
steps.code: java -XX:+UnlockDiagnosticVMOptions -XX:+PrintInlining -cp app.jar com.acme.pay.Main | grep requireAmount

steps.say: C2's line names the method, its bytecode size and the reason. too big means the call site isn't hot and the callee is over 35 bytes. hot method too big would mean a hot site and a callee over 325 bytes.
Look at what the 49 bytes are. javap -c -p shows the boxing calls, the varargs array and String.format that build the message. All of that is the cold path.
steps.code: javap -c -p -cp app.jar com.acme.pay.Guards | grep -A 30 'long requireAmount'

steps.say: Move the cold path into its own method and return the exception from it, so the hot method still ends in throw. Self-check before reading on: why return the exception instead of throwing it inside the helper? (Answer: with throw badAmount(cents), javac and the reader can see that the method ends there. A helper that throws by itself looks like an ordinary call that returns.)
steps.code: static long requireAmount(long cents) { if (cents <= 0 || cents > MAX_CENTS) throw badAmount(cents); // hot path: 21 bytes return cents; } static IllegalArgumentException badAmount(long cents) { // cold path, its own method return new IllegalArgumentException( String.format("amount must be between 1 and %d cents, got %d", MAX_CENTS, cents)); }

alt.html: fun requireAmount(cents: Long): Long { if (cents <= 0 || cents > MAX_CENTS) throw badAmount(cents) // hot path: 21 bytes return cents } fun badAmount(cents: Long) = // cold path, its own function IllegalArgumentException("amount must be between 1 and %d cents, got %d".format(MAX_CENTS, cents))

steps.say: Run the same command again. The hot method is 21 bytes and C2 inlines it. Keep the message text identical, because someone's alerting or log search may match on it.

lab.title: Fit two hot guards into the inlining budget
steps: Run the tests. Two pass (the guards behave correctly) and two fail: requireAmount is 49 bytes of bytecode and requireIdempotencyKey is 68. The limit in the test is 35, C2's MaxInlineSize.
Check the sizes yourself: after a build, run javap -c -p -cp performance/build/classes/java/main workbench.performance.l02.PaymentGuards. The offset of the last instruction plus one is the size.
Move the message building out of requireAmount into a private static method that returns the exception. Keep the exact message.
Do the same for requireIdempotencyKey. The null case must still say got null.
Run the tests until all four pass. The test reads the compiled class file, so BytecodeSize.java in the test folder shows exactly what it measures.
hints: The shape that fits: if (bad) throw badAmount(cents); return cents;. Everything about the message goes in badAmount.
String.format with two arguments costs a lot of bytecode: an array, two boxing calls and the call itself. In the cold method that doesn't matter.
In requireIdempotencyKey, the key == null ? "null" : ... choice belongs in the cold method too. Pass the key itself to the helper.
Both fixed methods come out at 21 and 27 bytes in the reference solution.

drill.title: Split a guard from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write a guard requireCurrency(String code) that returns code when it is exactly 3 characters long, and otherwise throws IllegalArgumentException("currency must be 3 letters, got '" + code + "'"). Shape it so the hot method stays small. Then write down the two C2 size limits and when each applies.

answer.html: static String requireCurrency(String code) { if (code == null || code.length() != 3) throw badCurrency(code); // hot: a check and a call return code; } private static IllegalArgumentException badCurrency(String code) { // cold: everything else return new IllegalArgumentException("currency must be 3 letters, got '" + code + "'"); } // C2 inlines up to 35 bytes of bytecode at a call site that runs on fewer than 25% of the // caller's invocations (MaxInlineSize), and up to 325 bytes at a hot one (FreqInlineSize).

alt.html: fun requireCurrency(code: String?): String { if (code == null || code.length != 3) throw badCurrency(code) // hot: a check and a call return code } private fun badCurrency(code: String?) = // cold: everything else IllegalArgumentException("currency must be 3 letters, got '$code'") // C2 inlines up to 35 bytes of bytecode at a call site that runs on fewer than 25% of the // caller's invocations (MaxInlineSize), and up to 325 bytes at a hot one (FreqInlineSize).

recap: C2 inlines a callee only within a bytecode budget: 35 bytes at call sites that aren't hot, 325 bytes at hot ones (25% of the caller's calls). Cold error paths count too, so give them their own method.
At each interface or virtual call, C2 uses the receiver types tier 3 recorded. One or two types get inlined behind type checks. Three or more without a 90% winner become a plain virtual call.
Whatever the profile never saw becomes an uncommon trap. When one fires, the frame goes back to the interpreter, the code is made not entrant, and the method is recompiled with the new case.
-XX:+UnlockDiagnosticVMOptions -XX:+PrintInlining and -Xlog:deoptimization=debug show these decisions. inline (hot) is just C2's success message.
Intrinsics (@IntrinsicCandidate) swap JDK methods such as Math.addExact, Arrays.equals and Long.bitCount for hand-written code. Kotlin's standard library reaches the same ones.

explain.prompt: A colleague asks: "Why did our settlement loop get slower when we added a third payment method, even though the new class is tiny?" Explain it in your own words.
explain.answer: The loop calls feeCents through the PaymentMethod interface. While only cards and SEPA reached that call, C2 inlined both implementations behind type checks, and could then optimize the loop body as a whole. It compiled any other type as an uncommon trap. When the first wallet payment arrived, the trap fired, the compiled code was thrown away and the method was recompiled. With three types and none above 90%, the call site is megamorphic, so C2 now emits a virtual call for every element and inlines nothing. The size of the new class doesn't matter. What changed is the number of types reaching that one call.

deeper.html:
Inlining is what makes escape analysis work. C2 can only prove that an object never leaves a method if it can see every method the object is passed to. A Money value created in a hot method and passed to a callee that isn't inlined has escaped, so it gets allocated on the heap. The memory track looks at escape analysis from the allocation side.

For experiments, -XX:CompileCommand=dontinline,com.acme.pay.Guards::requireAmount and -XX:CompileCommand=inline,... force a decision for one method, and the inlining log says force inline by CompileCommand. Use them to test a theory, not as a production fix.

One result here surprised me. I expected a shared helper such as static long timed(LongSupplier work) to make its work.getAsLong() call megamorphic when three different lambdas pass through it. C2 inlined all three anyway. Once it had inlined timed into each caller, it knew the exact lambda class at each spot and didn't need the shared profile. Megamorphic sites come from types that C2 can't see at compile time, such as objects read from an array, a field or a collection.

Other messages you'll meet in the log: inlining too deep (more than 15 levels, MaxInlineLevel), already compiled into a big method (a callee already compiled into more than 2,500 bytes of machine code), hot method too big (a hot site, over 325 bytes) and no static binding (C1 can't inline a virtual call). JITWatch shows the same information per method if the raw log gets too long.
